questions.question: According to the TR1 introduction, how is this technical report positioned?

options.A: A scientific guide and integrated overview that does not intend to establish a standard for sterilization validation
options.B: A mandatory standard endorsed by FDA that replaces regional regulatory requirements
options.C: A document that applies only to the EU market and is dedicated to interpreting EU regulations
options.D: An operating manual focused on hospital and laboratory sterilization that does not address manufacturing

questions.explanation: The introduction states that the task force aimed to write a scientific report usable across regulatory environments, to be regarded as a guide, not intended to establish a standard for sterilization validation, and serving as a single-source overview that supplements existing documents. It is not a mandatory standard and is not specific to one region; its scope is mainly manufacturing and it explicitly excludes non-CGMP applications such as hospitals and laboratories.

questions.question: Which of the following is WITHIN the scope of TR1?

options.A: Validation of steam sterilization of instruments in a hospital central supply department
options.B: Validation of facilities, utility systems, and equipment maintenance
options.C: Qualification of QC laboratory analytical methods, analytical instruments, and laboratory sterilizers
options.D: Change control, system suitability, and periodic requalification

questions.explanation: §1.1 states that Section 6.0 Ongoing controls covers change control, system suitability, and periodic requalification. The report explicitly is not intended for non-CGMP applications such as laboratories or hospitals, and does not cover facilities, equipment, maintenance, utilities, or analytical qualification.

questions.question: According to the glossary, for a BI with z = 10°C, which square wave exposure is equivalent to F0 = 8 minutes?

options.A: 116°C for 8 minutes
options.B: 121°C for 25.9 minutes
options.C: 116°C for about 25.9 minutes
options.D: 116°C for about 12 minutes

questions.explanation: F0 is calculated with Tref of 121.1°C (simplified to 121°C in the report) and z = 10°C. 116°C is about 5°C below the reference temperature, giving a lethal rate of about 0.31, so about 25.9 minutes is needed to accumulate an F0 of 8 minutes. 116°C for 8 minutes or for 12 minutes is not enough; 121°C for 25.9 minutes gives an F0 of about 25 minutes, far above 8.

questions.question: According to TR1 definitions, how does the handling of a failure to meet a critical parameter differ from a failure to meet a key parameter?

options.A: Both require the load to be rejected outright, with no release after investigation
options.B: Failing a critical parameter requires rejection; failing a key parameter requires investigation and documented rationale for disposition
options.C: Failing a critical parameter requires investigation and a decision; failing a key parameter requires only a note in the record
options.D: Both require only an investigation, and the load can be released as long as the BI is negative

questions.explanation: Critical parameters relate to product safety and efficacy, and a failure to meet them requires rejection of the load; key parameters are used to ensure the sterilization run stays in a state of control, and a failure requires an investigation and a documented rationale for the disposition. "Both require the load to be rejected" conflates the two, "investigation for critical and a note for key" reverses them, and "release as long as the BI is negative" ignores the rejection requirement for critical parameters.
questions.reference: PDA TR1 §2.0 Glossary (Operating / Critical / Key Parameters)

questions.question: How is Half-Cycle Qualification in the glossary performed?

options.A: Validate with half the exposure time, then double the physical and biological lethality values to extrapolate to the full cycle
options.B: Run only half the number of validation batches and complete the remainder during routine production
options.C: Cut the sterilization temperature in half to simulate the worst-case heat input
options.D: Place BIs in only half of the probe locations, with only temperature probes in the remaining locations

questions.explanation: Half-cycle qualification demonstrates cycle efficacy using 50% of the exposure time and doubles the physical and biological lethality values obtained from the half cycle to estimate the lethality the full cycle will deliver. It has nothing to do with the number of validation batches, halving the temperature, or the number of BI locations.

questions.question: Which statement about the D_T-value is correct?

options.A: It is a genetic constant of the species and is exactly the same regardless of carrier, suspending medium, or recovery and culture conditions
options.B: It represents the minutes required to reduce the population by 99% (2-log)
options.C: It is determined experimentally using a first-order survivor curve model and describes the resistance of a BI system
options.D: It is independent of temperature, so the reference temperature need not be stated when citing it

questions.explanation: D_T is the time required for a 1-log (90%) reduction in the population under specific lethal conditions, and is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the survivor curve. TR1 specifically emphasizes that the D-value is not simply a genetic property but is determined experimentally using a first-order model to describe the resistance of the BI challenge system, and is affected by carrier and environment. A D-value must also state its reference temperature (for example D121°C).

questions.question: A BI has N0 = 10^6 and D121°C = 2.5 minutes. If the physical parameters give F = 30 minutes, what NF is expected from the semilogarithmic model?

options.A: 10^0 (about 1 survivor per BI)
options.B: 10^-12 (equivalent to a 12-log survival probability)
options.C: 10^-3 (about one positive per thousand BIs)
options.D: 10^-6 (about one positive per million BIs)

questions.explanation: Log NF = −F/D + Log N0 = −30/2.5 + 6 = −6, so NF = 10^-6, meaning about a one-in-a-million chance that a BI is positive. 10^-12 results from forgetting to add back log N0; 10^0 and 10^-3 result from miscalculating the log reduction (30/2.5 = 12 log).

questions.question: A BI has z = 8°C and D121°C = 1.6 minutes. What is its approximate D-value at 113°C?

options.A: 16.0 minutes
options.B: 0.16 minutes
options.C: 3.2 minutes
options.D: 12.8 minutes

questions.explanation: The z-value is the temperature change needed to change the D-value tenfold. 113°C is 8°C below 121°C (exactly one z), so the D-value becomes 10 times larger, at 16.0 minutes; 0.16 minutes is the value at 8°C higher (129°C). 3.2 and 12.8 minutes are the incorrect results of a linear calculation.

questions.question: For a BI with z = 10°C, 1 minute at 120°C is equivalent to how many minutes at 121°C, and what does this illustrate?

options.A: About 0.90 minutes; a 1°C difference affects lethality by only about 10%
options.B: About 0.79 minutes; the exponential relationship reduces lethality by about 20%
options.C: About 0.50 minutes; each 1°C decrease halves lethality
options.D: 1.00 minute; anything within ±1°C is treated as fully equivalent

questions.explanation: L = 10^((T − Tref)/z) = 10^(−0.1) ≈ 0.79, so a difference of only 1°C reduces lethality by about 20%. This is why even small temperature fluctuations around the set point affect the F-value, and why F-value calculations convert all fluctuations into equivalent lethality. A 10% effect, a halving, or treating them as equivalent is not consistent with this exponential relationship.

questions.question: Why should fraction-negative methods (for example Holcomb-Spearman-Karber) not be used to evaluate BI kill results at different locations in a production sterilizer?

options.A: These methods cannot calculate confidence intervals for the D-value
options.B: BIs distributed throughout the chamber are not true replicates
options.C: Production sterilizer cycles cannot bring BIs into the quantal range
options.D: These methods require that BIs come from different lot numbers

questions.explanation: Statistical methods require that BIs be true replicates: the same lot, prepared the same way, recovered and cultured the same way, with exposure time as the only variable, and each replicate group receiving a similar dose, usually achieved with a resistometer. BIs at different locations in a production sterilizer cannot be guaranteed to receive the same lethality, so they are not replicates. The HSK method can in fact calculate confidence intervals, and BIs should come from the same lot, not different lots.

questions.question: According to TR1, which BI organisms are commonly used for cycle validation under the product-specific design approach?

options.A: Only Geobacillus stearothermophilus; no other organism is accepted
options.B: Vegetative organisms such as Bacillus atrophaeus and E. coli
options.C: Any strain isolated from the product, without heat resistance characterization
options.D: C. sporogenes, B. smithii, and B. subtilis 5230

questions.explanation: The overkill approach most commonly uses G. stearothermophilus; the product-specific approach commonly uses Clostridium sporogenes, Bacillus smithii (formerly B. coagulans), and Bacillus subtilis 5230. The microbiological challenge for steam sterilization should use only spores, and the spores should be clean and well characterized for heat response, so vegetative organisms and uncharacterized strains are not suitable.

questions.question: If the reliability of the BI supplier's CoA has been established through supplier qualification and the BI has not been modified, what does TR1 recommend for incoming testing?

options.A: The supplier's resistance values may be used, but the spore population should still be confirmed on receipt
options.B: Incoming testing can be waived entirely, with no confirmation of population or resistance
options.C: The D-value must be redetermined in-house for every lot, and the CoA cannot be relied on
options.D: Only package integrity need be checked; population and resistance rely entirely on the CoA

questions.explanation: When the reliability of the CoA is established and the BI is unmodified, the supplier's resistance values can replace lot-by-lot confirmation testing; however, considering the effects of shipping and handling, a spore population confirmation should still be performed on receipt, using the same counting method as the supplier to reduce variability. The stability of population and D-value over the BI's shelf life should also be evaluated.

questions.question: Which statement about chemical indicators and chemical integrators is correct?

options.A: Once validated, a chemical integrator can be used alone for cycle qualification
options.B: A chemical indicator only shows that a threshold temperature was reached, and does not mean the load is sterile
options.C: A chemical indicator can show the maximum temperature and the hold time
options.D: A chemical monitor can replace BIs and temperature measurement during validation

questions.explanation: A chemical indicator responds in a non-quantitative way, showing only that a threshold temperature was reached, not the maximum temperature or how long it was held, and it does not mean the load is sterile; it is mainly used to avoid confusing sterilized and unsterilized items. An integrator can respond quantitatively to time and temperature (sometimes humidity), but cannot be used alone for cycle qualification. Whatever the design, a chemical monitor cannot replace BIs and instrument-measured temperature, pressure, and time.

questions.question: According to TR1, which statement about the uses of the various steam types is correct?

options.A: Plant steam can be supplied directly to the chamber for porous/hard goods once filtered
options.B: Process steam contains volatile amine additives and can only supply the jacket
options.C: Sterilization of porous/hard goods loads should always use pure steam
options.D: Pure steam only needs condensate that meets Purified Water specifications

questions.explanation: Pure steam is steam whose condensate meets the WFI monograph, and sterilization of porous/hard goods loads should always use pure steam. Plant steam is generally suitable only for supplying the jacket (provided the chamber steam is not taken from the jacket) or for heating water on the non-sanitary side; process steam is generated from feed water without volatile additives such as amines and hydrazine and may be suitable for liquid loads.

questions.question: Which statement about superheated steam is correct?

options.A: Superheated steam is hotter, so actual lethality is better than the model predicts
options.B: The main cause is too much entrained liquid water in the steam
options.C: It affects only liquid loads and has no effect on porous/hard goods
options.D: It can be caused by excessive pressure reduction near the point of use or by a jacket hotter than the chamber

questions.explanation: At a given pressure, superheated steam is above the saturation curve in temperature, and its lethal effect is lower than predicted for that temperature because the semilogarithmic model assumes saturated steam. The main causes TR1 lists include excessive pressure reduction near the point of use and a jacket temperature higher than the chamber. Entrained liquid water is a wet steam/dryness value problem, and steam quality problems mainly affect porous/hard goods cycles.

questions.question: The overkill design approach requires F_PHY and F_BIO of at least 12 minutes. How is this figure derived?

options.A: Assuming N0 = 10^12 and D121°C = 1.0 minute, with a target survival of 10^0
options.B: Assuming N0 = 10^6 and D121°C = 1.0 minute, with a PNSU target of 10^-6
options.C: Assuming N0 = 10^6 and D121°C = 2.0 minutes, with a PNSU target of 10^0
options.D: Adopting directly the 121°C, 12 minutes that EU regulations define for terminal sterilization overkill

questions.explanation: Overkill assumes worst-case bioburden: N0 = 10^6, D121°C = 1.0 minute, z = 10°C, and to reach a PNSU of 10^-6, F = 1.0 × (6 − (−6)) = 12 minutes. The N0 = 10^12 and D121°C = 2.0 minutes pairs also multiply out to 12, but they are not the TR1 assumptions; the EU definition of overkill is 121°C for 15 minutes, not 12 minutes.

questions.question: In the product-specific design example, the design values are N0 = 10^2/unit and D_T = 0.4 minutes (only slightly above the bioburden resistance measured in the product). What are the minimum F0 needed for a PNSU of 10^-6 and the follow-up requirement?

options.A: 2.4 minutes; no follow-up bioburden monitoring needed
options.B: 8.0 minutes; only occasional periodic spot checks needed
options.C: 3.2 minutes; ongoing monitoring of bioburden population and resistance needed
options.D: 12 minutes; the safety margin is inadequate and the overkill approach must be used instead

questions.explanation: F = D × (log N0 − log NF) = 0.4 × (2 − (−6)) = 3.2 minutes. Because the design D-value is only slightly above the measured value and the safety margin is small, ongoing monitoring of bioburden population and resistance is needed to ensure there is no drift. If a very conservative D = 1.0 minute were used instead, F0 would be 8.0 minutes, and only then would the need for resistance testing be greatly reduced (though periodic monitoring is still advisable).

questions.question: According to TR1, what is the main basis for choosing between the overkill and product-specific design approaches?

options.A: Product-specific gives a higher sterility assurance level and should be preferred
options.B: The sterilizer type; prevacuum processes can only be paired with overkill
options.C: The regulatory region; the US uses overkill and the EU uses product-specific
options.D: The heat stability of the product or material being sterilized

questions.explanation: Both approaches can deliver the same sterility assurance level, and the choice depends mainly on the heat stability of the product or material. Product-specific requires more data on the item, the indicator organism, and the bioburden to allow a lower heat input, so it is better suited to terminal sterilization of heat-labile preparations. It has nothing to do with sterilizer type or regulatory region.

questions.question: In a prevacuum cycle that pulls the chamber down to 0.1 atm each time, approximately how much air do three vacuum pulses remove?

options.A: 99.9% (3-log reduction)
options.B: 90% (1-log reduction)
options.C: 99% (2-log reduction)
options.D: 99.9999% (6-log reduction)

questions.explanation: Each pull to 0.1 atm reduces the chamber air by 90% (1-log), so three pulses (with the corresponding steam charges) achieve a 3-log reduction, removing about 99.9% of the air. Positive pulses can also be added to condition the load, improving air removal and shortening equilibration time; the exact number and type of pulses should be determined during cycle development.

questions.question: Why must steam and air be continuously circulated when a steam-air mixture (SAM) process is used for liquid loads?

options.A: To bring the total chamber pressure below the saturated steam pressure to protect the containers
options.B: To expel all the air from the chamber before exposure
options.C: To avoid stratification and cold spots, and to reduce steam depletion near cold containers
options.D: To allow unsterilized cooling water to contact the containers directly as well

questions.explanation: SAM adds air to the steam so that the total pressure is above the saturation pressure, offsetting the expansion of heated headspace gas in the containers and maintaining container shape and seal integrity. Air reduces heat transfer, so the mixture must be continuously circulated (usually with a fan) to avoid stratification and cold spots in the load and to reduce steam depletion near cold containers. SAM does not remove air to begin with, and the total pressure is above, not below, the saturation pressure.

questions.question: How is equilibration time defined for porous/hard goods cycles, and what does an excessively long time indicate?

options.A: The time from the drain reaching temperature to the slowest probe reaching temperature; an excessive time indicates inadequate air removal or heating
options.B: The time from steam admission until the chamber reaches the set point; an excessive time indicates that the steam supply pressure is too high
options.C: The time of the entire exposure phase; an excessive time indicates too much safety margin in the cycle design
options.D: The time from the end of exposure until the door can be opened; an excessive time indicates inadequate vacuum drying

questions.explanation: Equilibration time is the time from when the chamber reference point (usually the drain) reaches the minimum specified sterilization temperature until the slowest-heating penetration probe in the load also reaches that temperature. It reflects the ability to remove air and to heat and condition the load; even if the temperature is eventually reached, an excessive time can still indicate inadequate air removal or heating. "The time from steam admission until the chamber reaches the set point" describes the chamber heat-up time. It can be shortened by adding pulses, drawing a deeper vacuum, adding hold steps, and so on.

questions.question: When preparing porous/hard goods items for saturated steam sterilization, which practice is consistent with TR1?

options.A: Wrap product contact surfaces in aluminum foil, which blocks microorganisms and is heat resistant
options.B: Use perforated boxes of stainless steel or anodized aluminum, and confirm that the vents remain open
options.C: Wrap extra turns of sterilization tape to make sure the wrapping does not loosen during sterilization
options.D: Switch to ordinary aluminum containers because they conduct heat well and heat up faster

questions.explanation: Wrapping must allow steam to penetrate (so that air and condensate can escape) while providing a non-shedding microbial barrier. Non-permeable materials such as aluminum foil and glassine paper should not be used for saturated steam sterilization; sterilization tape should be used sparingly; metal containers should be stainless steel or anodized aluminum, and ordinary aluminum generates particulates and should not be used. Before sterilization, confirm that the vents are in the open position and are not blocked by the wrapping.

questions.question: Which statement about cold-spot mapping of liquid containers is consistent with TR1?

options.A: Cold-spot mapping must be performed for every SVP (≤ 100 mL)
options.B: The cold spot of an LVP is always in the headspace at the top of the container
options.C: The cold spot of an LVP (> 100 mL) is usually between the geometric center and the bottom, and should be confirmed
options.D: When containers rotate during the process, the cold spot is fixed at the exact center of the container

questions.explanation: The cold spot of an LVP is typically on the vertical axis between the geometric center and the bottom of the product, and should be confirmed. Cold-spot mapping is generally not performed for SVPs because the solution heats up at almost the same rate as the sterilizer. Container orientation affects cold-spot location; when containers are rotated or tumbled, there may be no identifiable cold spot at all.

questions.question: During cycle development, a BI with N0 = 3 × 10^6 and D = 2.5 minutes is used to evaluate whether F_PHY and F_BIO agree, and an F_PHY of about 21.2 minutes is expected to bring the BI to a PNSU of 10^-2. If the actual BI positive rate is clearly higher than 1/100, what does it mean?

options.A: The BI resistance is low, and a BI with a smaller D-value should be used
options.B: The physical measurements overestimated lethality, and the cycle can simply be shortened
options.C: The result is normal, because F_BIO cannot be measured under these conditions anyway
options.D: The actual biological lethality is lower than the physical prediction, possibly indicating a problem with steam delivery

questions.explanation: By Equation 1, [log(3×10^6) − log(10^-2)] × 2.5 ≈ 21.2 minutes. If the actual biological lethality is lower than predicted from the physical measurements, the BI positive rate will be higher than 1/100, indicating there may be a problem with delivery of the lethal agent (steam), and the cause of the discrepancy should be found and corrected. A high BI positive rate does not mean the BI resistance is low, nor is it a basis for shortening the cycle.

questions.question: What does TR1 require for a stability study of a terminally sterilized product?

options.A: It is required regardless of design approach, with the product exposed to worst-case heat input conditions
options.B: It is required only for overkill, because product-specific already takes heat stability into account
options.C: It is enough to expose the product to the standard cycle at the set point
options.D: At the same F0, a higher temperature for a shorter time is always gentler, so no assessment is needed

questions.explanation: A stability study is required for terminally sterilized products regardless of which design approach is used. Sterilization and degradation reactions accumulate with time and temperature, and variation in heat-up and cool-down also affects stability, so the product should be exposed to worst-case heat input. At the same F0, a higher temperature for a shorter time is "considered" gentler on the product, but the actual effect still needs to be assessed.

questions.question: According to TR1, why does sterilization validation emphasize that physical and biological data must agree?

options.A: Physical data are sufficient, and BIs are added only to meet the regulatory form
options.B: As long as all BIs are negative, physical parameters need not be considered
options.C: Either one will do, depending on the type of sterilizer
options.D: Physical measurement alone is not enough for lumens, filters, and similar locations, and BI results need physical support

questions.explanation: Temperature and pressure measurements alone cannot confirm that lethal conditions were reached at locations where steam or heat penetrates with difficulty (for example a syringe lumen, needle shield, or filter); conversely, looking only at BI kill without considering the physical parameters needed to achieve it is also not enough to show the cycle is appropriate. Biological results should be broadly consistent with the physical data. In addition, initial qualification generally requires three consecutive successful runs for each load configuration.

questions.question: How should temperature distribution and heat penetration probes be placed?

options.A: Both types of probes are attached to the surface of load items to reflect the actual item temperature
options.B: Distribution probes are fixed to the shelves, and penetration probes are concentrated at the drain
options.C: Distribution probes are in the load area without touching items or hardware, and penetration probes are placed at the cold spot
options.D: Distribution probes are placed inside containers, and penetration probes are suspended in the chamber

questions.explanation: Temperature distribution confirms that the heating medium is uniformly distributed in the load area, so probes should be within the load area but not touch load items or hardware such as carts, shelves, and trays. Heat penetration confirms that energy is delivered into the items, with probes placed at the cold spot of liquid containers or at the slowest-heating location of porous/hard goods; liquid loads are also distributed randomly or geometrically and include known cold and hot zones.

questions.question: A product-specific design requires a minimum F_BIO of 6.0 minutes, and the qualification plan uses a BI with D = 1.2 minutes and expects complete kill (NF = 10^0). What should the minimum starting population N0 of the BI be?
questions.explanation: Log N0 = F/D + Log NF = 6.0/1.2 + 0 = 5, so N0 = 10^5. The MAC must completely kill a BI with N0 = 10^5 and D = 1.2 minutes to demonstrate F_BIO ≥ 6.0 minutes. The calculation uses the minimum required lethality; the F-value the MAC actually delivers is usually higher.

questions.question: When qualifying an overkill cycle by the half-cycle method using a BI with D = 1.0 minute, what population must the half cycle (half the MAC exposure time) kill at minimum?

options.A: 10^6, demonstrating F_BIO ≥ 6 for the half cycle and ≥ 12 minutes for the full cycle
options.B: 10^12, because the full cycle requires a 12-log reduction
options.C: 10^3, because the exposure time is only half that of the full cycle
options.D: 10^6, demonstrating that the half cycle itself already achieves F_BIO ≥ 12 minutes

questions.explanation: The half-cycle method requires an F_BIO of at least 6.0 minutes from half the MAC exposure time; 6.0 / 1.0 = 6, so a 10^6 BI must be killed, and after doubling, this demonstrates a full-cycle F_BIO ≥ 12 minutes. The half cycle itself needs only ≥ 6 minutes, not 12; 10^12 and 10^3 both miscalculate the log count.

questions.question: With the same sterilization parameters, which combinations should be qualified to cover liquid containers of similar design but different sizes and fill volumes by bracketing?

options.A: Only the most commonly produced container size and fill volume
options.B: The smallest container with the largest fill, and the largest container with the smallest fill
options.C: Only the single combination of the largest container with the largest fill
options.D: The largest container with the largest fill, and the smallest container with the smallest fill

questions.explanation: §5.5.2 states that qualifying the largest container with the largest fill, and the smallest container with the smallest fill, covers the sizes and fill volumes in between. Bracketing must use a scientific rationale or heat penetration and microbiological studies to identify the configurations that represent the range; qualifying only the common size, cross-pairing, or a single endpoint is not what this section describes for container size and fill volume.

questions.question: What does TR1 require for operating parameter review when releasing a routine sterilization load?

options.A: Parameters need to be reviewed only for products released by parametric release
options.B: A failure to meet a key parameter always means rejection, with no rationale required
options.C: All critical parameters must be met; if a key parameter is not met, a scientific rationale is needed to release
options.D: Parameter review can be skipped as long as a sterility test will be performed later

questions.explanation: Release must show that the qualified critical and key parameters were achieved in the routine cycle. All critical parameters must be met for release; key parameters better reflect the state of control, and if one is not met, a scientifically sound rationale must support release. Parameter review cannot be omitted whether the product is released by parametric release, followed by a sterility test, or further processed after sterilization.

questions.question: In a saturated steam prevacuum process, what is the role of a properly qualified air detector in system suitability?

options.A: It can support release of porous/hard goods and may reduce the need for leak and air removal tests
options.B: It can fully replace temperature and pressure records as the sole basis for releasing porous/hard goods loads
options.C: It is used mainly for liquid loads, detecting residual air in the container headspace
options.D: It must be installed at the top of the chamber to detect residual air

questions.explanation: Air detector results supported by development or qualification testing can be used to support release of porous/hard goods loads in a prevacuum process, and may reduce the need for chamber leak tests and air removal tests. It is usually installed near the sterilizer drain, and not every sterilizer has one; it is part of system suitability and cannot replace routine operating parameter review.

questions.question: According to TR1, which of the following changes is generally NOT considered a major change?

options.A: Changing the design of product racks or trays and the arrangement of the load in the chamber
options.B: Changing the operating or control mode of the sterilizer
options.C: Changing the product packaging or formulation
options.D: A like-for-like part replacement with no effect on performance

questions.explanation: Like-for-like replacement of sterilizer system parts is generally not considered a major change as long as it is shown that sterilizer performance is not affected. Chamber modifications, rack/tray design, load arrangement, changes to sterilizing medium supply and distribution, or changes to the operating/control mode may require temperature distribution, heat penetration, or microbiological challenge studies; changes to product design, materials, mass, formulation, or packaging may also require requalification.

questions.question: According to TR1, which statement about periodic requalification is correct?

options.A: Every 3 years, and the acceptance criteria of the original qualification may be relaxed
options.B: Usually every 12 months, using the parameters and acceptance criteria of the original qualification
options.C: Only when a deviation occurs, with no fixed frequency
options.D: Every 12 months, but only temperature distribution needs to be performed

questions.explanation: Requalification should be performed periodically (usually every 12 months) to ensure there are no undetected changes in the product or process, using the same operating parameters and acceptance criteria as the original qualification; for porous/hard goods loads, steam quality should also be confirmed. Event-driven requalification falls under change control (§6.3) and is a separate matter from periodic requalification.

questions.question: Besides repeating the qualification runs, what else should periodic requalification include?

options.A: Choosing only the load that is easiest to sterilize, to reduce the risk of failure
options.B: Redoing a product-specific bioburden D-value study
options.C: A review of trends in engineering, maintenance, and calibration data, and of change control records
options.D: Requalifying every product individually on every equivalent sterilizer

questions.explanation: Requalification should review performance data from monitoring sources such as engineering, maintenance, and calibration to confirm that there are no adverse trends or drift away from the validated baseline, and should also review change control documentation. Requalification should include the most difficult-to-sterilize load; if sterilizer equivalence has been established (§5.4), a reduced requalification may be considered, for example not requalifying every product on every sterilizer.
